records.quote:
"The world could do with a good deal more
mess, if you ask me," he said.
records.paraphrase: The painter voices disdain for the orderly society.

records.quote: about two hundred years old, sat on a stepladder
records.paraphrase: An old man is roughly two hundred years old.

records.quote:
Aging had
touched him that much before the cure for aging was found.
records.paraphrase: A cure for aging exists that halts further aging.

records.quote:
the Chicago Office of the Federal Bureau of
Termination
records.paraphrase: A government agency exists to manage terminations.

records.quote:
"He was
responsible for setting up the very first gas chamber in Chicago."
records.paraphrase: Leora admires Hitz for founding the first local gas chamber.

records.quote:
"Your city thanks you; your country
thanks you; your planet thanks you. But the deepest thanks of all is
from future generations."
records.paraphrase: The termination hostess frames suicide as a civic gift to the future.

records.quote:
There were no prisons, no slums, no insane asylums, no cripples, no
poverty, no wars.
records.paraphrase: The world has eliminated many longstanding social ills.

records.quote: Death, barring accidents, was an adventure for volunteers.
records.paraphrase: Death now occurs only by accident or voluntary choice.

records.quote:
In the year 2000," said Dr. Hitz, "before scientists stepped in and
laid down the law, there wasn't even enough drinking water to go around,
and nothing to eat but sea-weed
records.paraphrase: Past overpopulation caused water and food shortages until scientists intervened.

records.quote: He knew that he would never paint again.
records.paraphrase: The painter decides to stop painting after the killings.

records.quote:
they all sprouted mustaches
within five years or so.
records.paraphrase: Gas-chamber hostesses reportedly grow mustaches over time.

records.quote:
Wehling was fifty-six, a mere stripling in a population whose average
age was one hundred and twenty-nine.
records.paraphrase: Human lifespans are drastically extended, making 56 young.

records.quote: And then he shot himself, making room for all three of his children.
records.paraphrase: Wehling kills himself and Duncan to free space for his triplets.

records.quote: "I want those kids," said Wehling quietly. "I want all three of them."
records.paraphrase: Wehling states he wants to keep all three children.

records.quote: X-rays had revealed that his wife was going to have triplets.
records.paraphrase: Medical imaging revealed the pregnancy was triplets.

records.quote:
The law said that no newborn child could survive unless the parents of
the child could find someone who would volunteer to die.
records.paraphrase: Law requires a volunteer death for each new birth.

records.quote:
He was the only man
waiting. Not many people were born a day any more.
records.paraphrase: Births have become rare as a consequence of population control.

records.quote:
"A drupelet, Mr. Wehling, is one of the little knobs, one of the little
pulpy grains of a blackberry,"
records.paraphrase: Hitz explains overcrowding via a blackberry analogy.

records.quote:
The population of the United States was stabilized at forty-million
souls.
records.paraphrase: The national population is held fixed at forty million.

records.quote:
Would you like to go back to the good old days, when the population of
the Earth was twenty billion--about to become forty billion, then eighty
billion, then one hundred and sixty billion?
records.paraphrase: Hitz cites runaway population growth that prompted control.

records.quote:
All I have to do is pick
out which one of the triplets is going to live, then deliver my maternal
grandfather to the Happy Hooligan
records.paraphrase: Wehling bitterly describes having to choose which child lives.

records.quote:
"You think this is my idea of what life really looks
like?"
records.paraphrase: The painter contrasts the idealized mural with real life.

records.quote:
"To be or not to be" was the telephone number of the municipal gas
chambers of the Federal Bureau of Termination.
records.paraphrase: A phone number connects citizens to state-run gas chambers.

records.quote:
He corrected
himself, gave the municipal gas chambers their official title, a title
no one ever used in conversation. "I should have said, 'Ethical Suicide
Studios,'"
records.paraphrase: Euphemistic official naming contrasts with the grim reality of state killing.

records.quote: All diseases were conquered. So was old age.
records.paraphrase: Disease and aging have been cured.

records.quote:
The painter pondered the mournful puzzle of life demanding to be born
and, once born, demanding to be fruitful ... to multiply and to live as
long as possible--to do all that on a very small planet that would have
to last forever.
records.paraphrase: The painter reflects on the fundamental problem of reproduction on a finite planet.

records.quote:
He took Wehling's pistol, really intending to shoot himself.

But he didn't have the nerve.
records.paraphrase: The painter tries but cannot shoot himself.

records.quote:
Wehling shot Dr. Hitz dead. "There's room for one--a great big one," he
said.
records.paraphrase: Wehling murders Hitz to make room for a child.

criteria.rationale: The story is built on speculative biomedical science: all diseases conquered and a cure for aging found, producing an average population age of 129 and a two-hundred-year-old man. Scientific processes (population dynamics, drupelet/blackberry analogy, X-rays) materially ground the premise. Science is not decorative but the foundation of the world.

The engineered system of municipal gas chambers (Ethical Suicide Studios) run by the Federal Bureau of Termination is a technological/institutional apparatus central to the plot: it enforces the death-for-birth law and drives the climactic killings and the painter's final call.

The narrative is set in a speculative future United States after the year 2000 crisis, with a stabilized population of forty million and lifespans of centuries. The future setting is more than an incidental date; it defines the storyworld.

The whole story extrapolates from the premise of cured aging/disease plus a finite planet: overpopulation necessitates a one-death-per-birth law, rare births, and state termination. Social consequences are systematically developed from the identifiable scientific/social premise, the core of the satire.

Science is invoked expositionally (scientists 'stepped in and laid down the law,' X-ray diagnosis, the drupelet reasoning, the painter's contemplation of the finite-planet puzzle) but observation, hypothesis, testing, and evidential revision do not actively drive the characters' understanding or action within the story. It is reasoning-by-analogy and background rather than dramatized scientific method.

The story is set entirely on Earth (Chicago). Planetary imagery ('this old planet,' 'your planet thanks you') is metaphorical scale, not other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them.

A large-scale demographic catastrophe is remembered and causally central: runaway overpopulation toward twenty/forty/eighty/one hundred sixty billion, with water and food shortages ('nothing to eat but sea-weed') that prompted the entire population-control regime. The painter also recalls war, plague, and starvation. The individual shootings alone are personal, but the remembered global disaster drives the premise.
